findings.summary: The note on the code sample says Stats' resolvers never run, but that is only true when `$full` is false.
findings.fix: Change the note to "with $full: false, Stats' fields are skipped and their resolvers never run".

findings.summary: The page's opening concept, the inline fragment with no type condition used to group fields under one directive, is stated without any code example.
findings.evidence: "Drop `on Type` to group fields under one directive", "Saves repeating `@include` on every field", "Same tool, different job: grouping, not narrowing". The subtitle is "The unnamed spread", but the only code blocks on the page show named spreads (`...Header_user`, `...Stats @include(if: $full)`).
findings.fix: Add a short code block right after these bullets showing the untyped inline fragment, e.g. `viewer { id ... @include(if: $full) { email phone bio } }`, next to the repetitive per-field `@include` version it replaces.

findings.summary: The conditional-spread example sits under the Field Merging heading, but it shows conditional fetching rather than merging, so the learner can't tell which point it illustrates.
findings.evidence: Under "10. Field Merging": `...UserFields` / `...Stats @include(if: $full)` with note "Stats' resolvers never run". Nothing in the snippet selects the same response key twice, and nothing shows a merge or a conflict.
findings.fix: Move this code block up next to the directive-grouping bullets at the top, as a conditional-fetching example. Under Field Merging, put an example that actually merges, e.g. `...A ...B` where both select `name`, plus the conflicting case `avatar(size: 32)` vs `avatar(size: 64)`.

findings.summary: Two hashtags name specific languages that the content never mentions; GraphQL operations don't depend on any language.
findings.evidence: "#javascript", "#typescript" — caption covers directives, fragments, unions vs interfaces and field merging, with no JavaScript or TypeScript content
findings.fix: Replace #javascript and #typescript with GraphQL-relevant tags such as #graphqlschema and #graphqlfragments, or remove them.

findings.summary: The colocation callout says colocation fixes "the classic REST problem" without naming the problem, and that overstates what it does: GraphQL's selection sets deal with over- and under-fetching, while colocation keeps each component's data requirements next to the component.
findings.evidence: "This is the fix for the classic REST problem."
findings.fix: Replace it with "Components can't silently lose data they depend on when another component's query changes." You could also say it keeps one shared query from drifting out of sync with the components that use it.

findings.summary: The rule that conflicting arguments on one response key cause a validation error has no example, although the caption's hook depends on it.
findings.evidence: "Same key, **conflicting** args → validation error"; the caption says "Two fragments ask for the same field with different arguments, and the whole operation fails validation."
findings.fix: Add a two-fragment snippet, e.g. `fragment A on User { pic: avatar(size: 32) }` next to `fragment B on User { avatar(size: 64) }`, with the conflicting pair marked as the error.

findings.summary: The colocation callout relies on "the classic REST problem" without saying what that problem is, and REST comparisons only come later in the handbook (chapter 9).
findings.evidence: "This is the fix for the classic REST problem."
findings.fix: Name the problem inline, e.g. "In REST, a component's data needs live in a distant endpoint; colocation keeps them together." Or drop the REST reference.

findings.summary: The closing takeaway is about unions, but the page ends on field merging, so the last thing the learner reads before the takeaway is a different topic.
findings.evidence: The last sections are "10. Field Merging" and the Relay callout, followed by the takeaway "On a union, select only `__typename` directly; every other field goes inside a fragment."
findings.fix: Either put the union takeaway directly after the "9. Unions vs Interfaces" table as a tip, or change the final takeaway to summarize field merging (e.g. "Same response key must be mergeable — alias when it isn't").
